# Calculating (some) signals

Day 2, 15:30 · Google · coverage: transcript

## Claims

- **[Stage]** Among the many signals Google calculates during indexing, the ones singled out as having large effects on search results were country, language, freshness, SafeSearch and spam.
  <br><sub>`D2-C648` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works) · Extends [D1-C037](D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Country and language are among Google's most important signals and have been used since Google's early days.
  > "Both of them are extremely, extremely important"
  <br><sub>`D2-C649` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works) · Extended by [D3-C079](D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) · Extended by [D3-C082](D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Smaller languages have fewer documents on the web and so worse coverage, from an indexing perspective, than large ones, for example Basque compared with Spanish or Portuguese, Hungarian compared with German, and Sicilian compared with Italian.
  <br><sub>`D2-C650` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google detects the language of each document and weights language in index selection so that the index is not dominated by one or two languages.
  <br><sub>`D2-C651` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D2-C585](D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Without language or country input to index selection, Google's index would become an English index, because so many documents on the web are in English.
  > "if you just let the index decide what to rank without language or country input, then you would have an English index"
  <br><sub>`D2-C652` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google also takes country into account in index selection, so that countries producing less content in a shared language, such as the UK for English or Switzerland for German, are not disadvantaged against the US or Germany, which produce most of it.
  <br><sub>`D2-C653` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** In ranking, country and language signals help Google serve users the right content for their country and language.
  <br><sub>`D2-C654` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works), [Managing multi-regional and multilingual sites](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/managing-multi-regional-sites) · Extended by [D3-C006](D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) · Extended by [D3-C080](D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** A site serving a smaller country in a big language, such as British English or Swiss German, should make that country unmistakable (country-code domain or region-specific hreflang, local address, prices and currency) so its pages can benefit from index selection's country balancing instead of competing with the much larger US or German content pool.
  <br><sub>`D2-C655` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Calculating (some) signals · [Managing multi-regional and multilingual sites](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/managing-multi-regional-sites)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Freshness is a signal for queries that deserve fresh results ('query deserves freshness'): when a breaking event hits a city, such as possible closure of Barcelona's airport, users want really fresh results, not results from two weeks ago.
  <br><sub>`D2-C656` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [A guide to Google Search ranking systems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ranking-systems-guide) · Extends [D1-C045](D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Extended by [D3-C487](D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google calculates some freshness signals during indexing but uses them in ranking.
  <br><sub>`D2-C657` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works), [A guide to Google Search ranking systems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ranking-systems-guide)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Freshness plays no big role in index selection: whether a page was published 30 years ago or today makes no difference to its chance of being indexed.
  > "It doesn't play a big role in index selection."
  <br><sub>`D2-C658` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Changing a page's date or making cosmetic edits will not help an old page get indexed, because freshness plays no big role in index selection; freshness pays off only when ranking for queries that deserve fresh results.
  <br><sub>`D2-C659` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Calculating (some) signals</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google uses multiple systems to protect users from unexpected explicit results: its algorithms detect whether a user is looking for explicit content and rank results accordingly, so the aim is not to never show explicit results but to avoid showing them to users who are not looking for them.
  <br><sub>`D2-C660` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Guidelines for sites with explicit content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/safesearch)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Whether a page's content is explicit does not matter for indexing: judged on content type alone, an explicit page has the same chance of being indexed as a major news site's homepage.
  <br><sub>`D2-C661` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google calculates SafeSearch signals during indexing rather than in ranking, because ranking happens online with no time for such calculations, while indexing has the processing power.
  > "In ranking, everything has to happen online, and there's just not enough time to calculate those things."
  <br><sub>`D2-C662` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Calculating SafeSearch signals for a page needs its whole parsed HTML plus knowledge of which pages link to it and which pages it links to.
  <br><sub>`D2-C663` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Guidelines for sites with explicit content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/safesearch)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's guidelines for sites with explicit content recommend grouping explicit pages on a separate domain or subdomain; otherwise Google's systems may judge the whole site explicit and filter all of it when SafeSearch is on.
  <br><sub>`D2-C664` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Calculating (some) signals · is the documentation · [Guidelines for sites with explicit content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/safesearch) · Used by `DEV-IDX-12`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Because explicit content on its own does not lower a page's chance of being indexed, the practical risk for a site that mixes explicit and general content is SafeSearch classification, which looks at the whole page and its links; keep explicit pages on a separate domain or subdomain, as Google advises.
  <br><sub>`D2-C665` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Calculating (some) signals · [Guidelines for sites with explicit content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/safesearch) · Used by `DEV-IDX-12`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Spam stops a document at indexing: when Google detects that a document is spam, it does not let it into the index.
  > "If we detect that something is spam, then we're not letting it into the index."
  <br><sub>`D2-C666` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [How we fought spam on Google Search in 2022](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/04/webspam-report-2022)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's spam policies say that sites violating them may rank lower in results or not appear in results at all.
  <br><sub>`D2-C667` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Calculating (some) signals · is the documentation · [Spam policies for Google web search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) · Used by `DEV-HTM-06`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google uses more and more AI to detect spam, and Google's testing shows that this AI-based detection is highly accurate.
  <br><sub>`D2-C668` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Google Search spam updates and your site](https://developers.google.com/search/updates/spam-updates), [How we fought Search spam on Google in 2021](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2022/04/webspam-report-2021) · Extends [D1-C041](D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Extended by [D3-C205](D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) · Extended by [D3-C206](D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** SpamBrain, Google's AI-based spam detection system, is nowadays built on Gemini and fine-tuned specifically for finding spam.
  > "built on top of, well, nowadays, Gemini, and fine-tuned to that specific purpose of finding spam"
  <br><sub>`D2-C669` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs · Extends [D1-C041](D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Extends [D1-C039](D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) · Used by the glossary term *SpamBrain*</sub>

- **[Stage]** SpamBrain is central to Google's spam-fighting efforts and has been improved many times since its launch.
  <br><sub>`D2-C670` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [How we fought spam on Google Search in 2022](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/04/webspam-report-2022), [How we fought Search spam on Google in 2021](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2022/04/webspam-report-2021) · Extended by [D3-C287](D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's 2021 webspam report says SpamBrain, its AI-based spam-prevention system, was launched in 2018 and has been continuously improved since.
  <br><sub>`D2-C671` · Search Central blog (21 April 2022) · annotates Day 2, Calculating (some) signals · is the documentation · [How we fought Search spam on Google in 2021](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2022/04/webspam-report-2021) · Used by the glossary term *SpamBrain*</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The SpamBrain launch year mentioned on stage, with hesitation, was 2022, which does not match Google's documented 2018; 2022 is the year of the improvements described in Google's 2022 webspam report, so cite 2018 as the launch year.
  <br><sub>`D2-C672` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Calculating (some) signals</sub>

- **[Stage]** SpamBrain was said to detect 5 times more spam sites than the spam algorithms Google had launched before it.
  <br><sub>`D2-C673` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's 2022 webspam report says SpamBrain detected 5 times more spam sites in 2022 than in 2021, and 200 times more than when it first launched.
  <br><sub>`D2-C674` · Search Central blog (11 April 2023) · annotates Day 2, Calculating (some) signals · is the documentation · [How we fought spam on Google Search in 2022](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/04/webspam-report-2022)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The '5 times more spam sites' figure said on stage matches Google's 2022 webspam report, but the report compares 2022 with 2021 (and gives 200 times since launch), not SpamBrain with earlier algorithms; quote the documented comparison.
  <br><sub>`D2-C675` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Calculating (some) signals</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's testing shows that, thanks to SpamBrain, more than 99% of visits from Search are now spam-free.
  <br><sub>`D2-C676` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [How we fought spam on Google Search in 2022](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/04/webspam-report-2022) · Repeated by [D3-C275](D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Language, country, SafeSearch and spam signals, and some freshness signals, are calculated when a page is indexed, so a fix such as correcting a page's language or removing content that triggers SafeSearch only counts once Google recrawls and reprocesses the page; request recrawling of the most important URLs after the fix.
  <br><sub>`D2-C677` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Calculating (some) signals · Used by `DEV-IDX-12`, `DEV-MON-02`</sub>

- **[Stage]** Many of Google's signals are described in its developer documentation, though not always under the name 'signals'.
  <br><sub>`D2-C678` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [In-depth guide to how Google Search works](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/how-search-works), [A guide to Google Search ranking systems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ranking-systems-guide)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Combing Google's documentation for signals is not the best use of an SEO's time; creating content that users will like is a better one.
  > "If you are just focusing on actually creating the content that users will like, then that's probably a better use of your life."
  <br><sub>`D2-C679` · Day 2, Calculating (some) signals (Google) · Repeats [D1-C059](D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's guidelines for sites with explicit content say to mark each explicit page with rating markup set to adult, either as a meta tag named rating or as an HTTP response header.
  <br><sub>`D2-C837` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Calculating (some) signals · is the documentation · [Guidelines for sites with explicit content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/safesearch) · Used by `DEV-IDX-12`</sub>
